 Veterans Day: Remembering veterans beyond the holiday
 Ben Ko , Staff Writer 
 November 20, 2026 
 On Nov. 11, Americans observed Veterans Day, a federal holiday honoring those who have served in the U.S. military. It was originally known as Armistice Day until its purpose expanded in 1954 to honor American veterans of all wars.
 Veterans Day traces its origin to Nov. 11, 1918, when it was exclusive to those who served during World War I. However, as the United States became involved in additional wars, it brought new generations of veterans. In 1954, the name and meaning were changed into the Veterans Day we know today. While Veterans Day was expanded, the holiday’s significance ultimately depends on how people understand and recognize the service of veterans today.
 “People should be encouraged to talk with people who serve or think of people in their family or know people in their family and just think about what they have done for this country,” Eytan Alpert, freshman, said.
 Many students emphasize the importance of recognizing veterans beyond the holiday itself, through personal connections and greater public appreciation. Individuals can honor veterans by acknowledging their experiences and sacrifices.
 “More people should care about this holiday because it’s important to recognize those who have served our country and risked their lives,” Leonard Withrow, freshman, said.
 While recognizing and understanding are important aspects of the holiday, appreciation alone does not necessarily reflect the support they receive.
 “We (as a country) claim to support and honor veterans, but nearly 30,000 veterans have experienced unhoused conditions over the last 12 months,” Colin Sallee, English teacher, said. “Americans are less inclined to passively accept conflict and the narratives that create them; thus devaluing the celebration of veterans. This is unfortunate, because they deserve to be celebrated, largely.”
 Despite the holiday, questions remain about whether veterans receive the support they truly need throughout the year. For instance, recent statistics from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) indicate that at least 30% of veterans are in need of medical or mental health treatment. However, access to adequate care remains a challenge, specifically those dealing with conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). These issues raise questions about the gap between publicly recognizing veterans’ service and ensuring they receive the support they need.
 While statistics highlight challenges veterans face, hearing directly from them can provide a more personal understanding of their experiences.
 “We, as a community, should hold space for veterans to tell their stories. Why they served, what their experiences were, how it has impacted them, what they believe the holiday is and what it should be,” Sallee added.
 Creating opportunities for veterans to share their stories would allow students to understand military service beyond what they learn from textbooks. Hearing firsthand accounts could also help students recognize the experiences behind sacrifices Veterans Day commemorates.
 While schools can help students understand veterans through firsthand accounts, recognizing their service also requires involvement from the broader community. In Evanston, Veterans Day was celebrated at Fountain Square, led by the organization American Legion Post 42 and Veterans of Foreign Wars (VFW) Post 7186. Veterans shared stories with the community, reflected on their military service and emphasized the importance of preserving veteran history.
 Events like Evanston’s Veterans Day celebration can provide opportunities for communities to recognize veterans. However, honoring their service should extend beyond a single day. Through education, community recognition and support, Americans can ensure that appreciation for veterans is reflected throughout the year, rather than Nov. 11 alone.

 About the Contributor 
 Sam Zakarin , Photo Editor 
 Hi! I’m Sam Zakarin, I’m a Junior, and this year’s Photo Editor. This is my third year with The Evanstonian. I was a photographer my first two years. I love The Evanstonian’s photo section because of our community of photographers, which starts long-lasting relationships that reach well beyond the borders of photography. I have an array of jobs and internships as a photographer outside of school, and I enjoy doing street photography. I also like to read and play basketball.
